title: Analects
author: confucius
attributionNote: The Analects record sayings of Confucius and his disciples. They were compiled by followers over two centuries and contain several layers; the work is not an autograph by Confucius.
description: The Analects is the central book of Confucian ethics: twenty books of short sayings and exchanges on learning, ritual propriety, filial conduct, government and the formation of the exemplary person (junzi). Legge's translation is printed here book by book and chapter by chapter, with the Chinese text of the archive's bilingual page beside it, so a saying can be read in the translator's Victorian English and in the received Chinese at once.
historicalContext: The sayings took shape during the Warring States period and were edited into their present twenty books in the Han. Zhu Xi's twelfth-century selection of the Analects with the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean and Mencius fixed the Four Books that governed Chinese education and the imperial examinations from 1315. James Legge printed the Analects, with the Chinese text, his translation and his exegetical notes, as the first volume of The Chinese Classics (1893), the edition the archive transcribes here.
availabilityNote: Complete in Legge's translation: all twenty books and 496 numbered chapters, streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one book per chapter of the library's index. The Chinese is the same page's source text, which the archive transcribes for the first ten chapters of each book only; where the Chinese stops, the pane is empty. Legge's exegetical notes, his prolegomena and the volume's other apparatus are not part of the work.
